qs.q: Which spirometric profile is characteristic of obstructive lung diseases like chronic obstructive pulmonary disease?
o: Proportionately reduced FEV1 and FVC with a high ratio
Normal FVC and an increased FEV1 with normal ratio
Decreased FEV1/FVC ratio with significantly decreased FEV1
Significantly reduced FVC with a normal FEV1/FVC ratio
qs.e: Obstructive diseases show increased resistance to airflow, resulting in a significantly decreased FEV1 and an overall decreased FEV1/FVC ratio below 0.7. Restrictive diseases typically present with a normal or near normal FEV1/FVC ratio.

qs.q: What is the hallmark physiological finding that defines an obstructive lung disease?
qs.e: Obstructive lung diseases are characterized by increased resistance to airflow, which results in a decreased FEV1/FVC ratio. Restrictive diseases instead present with a reduced FVC while maintaining a near-normal ratio.

qs.q: During pulmonary function testing, a patient is evaluated for suspected airway obstruction. Which spirometric finding confirms an obstructive lung disease pattern such as asthma or COPD?
qs.e: Obstructive lung diseases such as asthma, COPD, and bronchiectasis are characterized by a decreased FEV1/FVC ratio. Restrictive diseases typically show a normal or increased FEV1/FVC ratio with reduced overall lung volumes.

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Obstructive lung diseases cause airflow limitation due to airway narrowing or loss of elastic recoil, shown by a reduced FEV1/FVC ratio. They range from asthma to COPD and require pattern‑recognition beyond memorisation.

sections.p: Obstructive lung disease is defined by a post‑bronchodilator FEV1/FVC < 0.70, indicating increased resistance to expiration. Diagnosis combines history, spirometry, and exclusion of restrictive patterns.
b: FEV1/FVC < 0.70 after bronchodilator
Symptoms: dyspnoea, chronic cough, wheeze

t.b: Does the patient have obstructive physiology? A reduced FEV1/FVC confirms obstruction; severity is graded by FEV1 % predicted.
Is airway calibre variable? Low or variable peak flow suggests asthma rather than fixed COPD.

sections.p: GOLD stages COPD by post‑bronchodilator FEV1 % predicted; asthma severity uses symptom frequency and exacerbation history. Staging guides therapy intensity.
b: GOLD 1: FEV1 ≥ 80 % predicted
GOLD 2: 50‑79 % predicted
GOLD 3: 30‑49 % predicted
GOLD 4: < 30 % predicted

sections.p: Identify the underlying process that narrows airways or destroys alveolar walls.
b: Smoking‑related COPD (emphysema, chronic bronchitis)
Allergic asthma (atopy, viral triggers)
Bronchiectasis from recurrent infection (TB, HIV, post‑pneumonia)
Occupational exposures (dust, biomass fuel)
Alpha‑1 antitrypsin deficiency (early emphysema, especially in non‑smokers)

sections.p: Patients report progressive dyspnoea, chronic cough with sputum, wheeze, and reduced exercise tolerance. Acute worsening (exacerbation) presents with increased sputum purulence and breathlessness.
b: Dyspnoea on exertion → early sign
Productive cough → chronic bronchitis
Wheeze that improves with bronchodilator → asthma

sections.p: Select tests that answer specific clinical questions; adapt when resources are limited.

t.b: Is there hyperinflation or other lung pathology? Hyperlucent lungs support emphysema; infiltrates suggest infection.
Is bronchiectasis present? Dilated airways on CT confirm diagnosis when X‑ray is equivocal.
Is early‑onset emphysema due to deficiency? Low level confirms genetic cause; if unavailable, consider family history and early disease in non‑smokers.
Is eosinophilic inflammation driving asthma/COPD? Elevated eosinophils suggest benefit from inhaled steroids.

sections.p: Recognise features that signal imminent deterioration or life‑threatening events.
b: Sudden worsening of dyspnoea with silent chest → possible pneumothorax
Persistent hypoxaemia (SpO2 < 88 %) despite therapy → respiratory failure
Cor pulmonale signs (jugular venous distension, peripheral oedema) → right‑heart strain

sections.p: Treat the aetiology first, then provide bronchodilation, anti‑inflammatory therapy, and supportive measures. Avoid unnecessary antibiotics unless infection is proven.
b: Smoking cessation – the single most effective intervention for COPD
Inhaled bronchodilators (short‑acting β2‑agonist, long‑acting anticholinergic) – open airways, improve symptoms
Inhaled corticosteroids – indicated for asthma and COPD with frequent exacerbations or high eosinophils
Vaccinations (influenza, pneumococcal) – prevent infectious triggers
Pulmonary rehabilitation – improves exercise capacity

sections.p: Regular review of symptoms, spirometry, and inhaler technique prevents exacerbations and slows decline.
b: Spirometry every 1‑2 years to track FEV1 decline
Action plan for early recognition of exacerbations
Education on avoidance of biomass smoke and occupational irritants

sections.p: Conditions that can mimic obstructive patterns on presentation or testing.
b: Restrictive lung disease with a normal FEV1/FVC (e.g., interstitial fibrosis)
Heart failure causing dyspnoea but normal spirometry
Vocal cord dysfunction producing wheeze without airflow limitation
FEV1/FVC may appear normal in early disease; look for reduced FEV1 trend.
Chest X‑ray can be normal in early COPD; rely on spirometry.
Eosinophil count can be transiently low during steroid use, masking asthma phenotype.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe breathlessness or chest pain
Confusion or inability to speak full sentences

faq.q: Why is the FEV1/FVC ratio used to define obstruction?
faq.a: It compares the speed of forced exhalation to total lung capacity; a low ratio shows that expiration is disproportionately slowed.
Yes, especially with biomass fuel exposure, alpha‑1 antitrypsin deficiency, or repeated infections.

faq.q: When is inhaled corticosteroid therapy appropriate in COPD?
faq.a: When the patient has frequent exacerbations or an eosinophil count >300 cells/µL, indicating an inflammatory component.

exam: Explain how spirometry differentiates obstructive from restrictive lung disease and list the GOLD staging criteria.
